section.title: Idolaters Condemned
section.sectionRationale: Elders come to Ezekiel seeking a word from the LORD while carrying idols in their own hearts, exposing a hypocrisy far deeper than outward idol worship. God answers their inquiry by naming the idolatry hidden behind their pious posture, then widens the lens to a sobering principle: even the greatest intercessors in Israel's memory, Noah, Daniel, and Job, could not save anyone but themselves from a land under righteous judgment.
section.thesis: God exposes idols set up in the heart as the deepest form of idolatry, refuses to be consulted by those who cling to them, and declares that when judgment justly falls on a land, even the righteousness of Noah, Daniel, and Job could deliver only themselves, not others, a truth that makes the substitutionary righteousness of Christ, who alone can deliver others by His own, all the more astonishing.
section.frameNote: Three movements: elders with idols in their hearts come to inquire of the LORD, and God exposes and answers their hidden idolatry directly; the sobering principle that Noah, Daniel, and Job could rescue only themselves, not their own children, from a land under deserved judgment; and the assurance that a remnant will survive to bring comfort by the very sight of their sobered conduct.

verses.text: Then some of the elders of Israel came and sat down before me.
And the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, these men have set up {{gillulim|idols}} in their hearts and put wicked stumbling blocks before their faces. Should I consult with them in any way?

Therefore speak to them and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘When any Israelite sets up idols in his heart and puts a wicked stumbling block before his face, and then comes to the prophet, I the LORD will answer him according to his great idolatry,
so that I may take hold of the hearts of the people of Israel. For because of their idols, they are all estranged from Me.’
Therefore tell the house of Israel that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Repent and turn away from your idols; turn your faces away from all your abominations.

For when any Israelite or any foreigner dwelling in Israel separates himself from Me, sets up idols in his heart, and puts a wicked stumbling block before his face, and then comes to the prophet to inquire of Me, I the LORD will answer him Myself.
I will set My face against that man and make him a sign and a proverb; I will cut him off from among My people. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
But if the prophet is enticed to speak a message, then it was I the LORD who enticed him, and I will stretch out My hand against him and destroy him from among My people Israel.
They will bear their punishment, the punishment of the inquirer will be the same as that of the prophet,

in order that the house of Israel may no longer stray from Me and no longer defile themselves with all their transgressions. Then they will be My people and I will be their God, declares the Lord GOD.’”

units.label: Noah, Daniel, and Job
units.note: righteousness that can save only itself

verses.text: And the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, if a land sins against Me by acting unfaithfully, and I stretch out My hand against it to cut off its supply of food, to send famine upon it, and to cut off from it both man and beast,
then even if these three men, {{tsedaqah|Noah, Daniel, and Job}}, were in it, their righteousness could deliver only themselves, declares the Lord GOD.
Or if I send wild beasts through the land to leave it childless and desolate, with no man passing through it for fear of the beasts,
then as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, even if these three men were in it, they could not deliver their own sons or daughters. They alone would be delivered, but the land would be desolate.
Or if I bring a sword against that land and say, ‘Let a sword pass through it,’ so that I cut off from it both man and beast,
then as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, even if these three men were in it, they could not deliver their own sons or daughters. They alone would be delivered.
Or if I send a plague into that land and pour out My wrath upon it through bloodshed, cutting off from it both man and beast,
then as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were in it, they could not deliver their own sons or daughters. Their righteousness could deliver only themselves.

units.label: A remnant left for comfort
units.note: the four dire judgments and the surviving witnesses

verses.text: For this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘How much worse will it be when I send against Jerusalem My four dire judgments: sword, famine, wild beasts, and plague, in order to cut off from it both man and beast?

Yet, behold, some survivors will be left in it, sons and daughters who will be brought out. They will come out to you, and when you see their conduct and actions, you will be comforted regarding the disaster I have brought upon Jerusalem, all that I have brought upon it.
They will bring you consolation when you see their conduct and actions, and you will know that it was not without cause that I have done all these things within it,’ declares the Lord GOD.”

gillulim.gloss: Idols, a term of deliberate contempt related to the word for dung pellets, used almost exclusively by Ezekiel to describe false gods. Here the idols are not physical statues but are 'set up in the heart', showing that outward compliance can hide inward, entrenched idolatry.

tsedaqah.gloss: Righteousness. The righteousness of Noah, Daniel, and Job, three men famous across the ancient world for uprightness and effective intercession, is here declared powerful enough to save only themselves, not even their own children, when judgment justly falls on a land.

basic.context: Elders come to Ezekiel seeking a word from God while secretly carrying idols in their hearts, and God exposes their hypocrisy before answering. He then widens the scope with a sobering principle: even if the three most righteous men Israel remembered, Noah, Daniel, and Job, stood in a land under deserved judgment, their righteousness could rescue only themselves, never anyone else.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a direct, historical confrontation with specific elders and a general theological principle about corporate judgment, not an abstract philosophical exercise. The hardest truth here is double: outward religious behavior can mask deep idolatry, and even the greatest human righteousness has real limits, it cannot be transferred to save someone else.
basic.originalLanguages: These men have set up gillulim, idols, a term of deliberate contempt, in their very hearts, showing that idolatry is fundamentally an inward condition before it is ever an outward statue. Even the tsedaqah, righteousness, of Noah, Daniel, and Job, three legendary examples of uprightness, is declared insufficient to deliver anyone but themselves from a land under God's righteous hand.
basic.typology: The stark limitation that even Noah, Daniel, and Job could deliver only themselves highlights, by deliberate contrast, the uniqueness of Christ, whose righteousness, unlike theirs, genuinely does deliver others, since 'by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous', Romans 5:19.
basic.christ: Where Noah, Daniel, and Job stand as the ceiling of merely human righteousness, unable to rescue even their own children, Christ is revealed as the one righteous man whose obedience actually does avail for others, Isaiah 53:11, Romans 5:19, 2 Corinthians 5:21; He is the true intercessor these three could only foreshadow, able to save not only Himself but everyone who trusts in Him.
basic.god: God is discerning beyond mere outward appearance, seeing straight through pious postures to idols hidden in the heart; He is also scrupulously just, holding a land accountable for genuine, deserved sin, while still, remarkably, preserving a remnant whose visible transformation will bring comfort even amid deserved judgment.
basic.crossReferences: Ezekiel 18 develops further this principle of individual responsibility before God. Romans 5:19 contrasts the disobedience of one man with the obedience of one man, Christ, that makes many righteous. Isaiah 53:11 says the Righteous One will justify many by bearing their iniquities. 2 Corinthians 5:21 declares He became sin for us so we might become His righteousness.
basic.oneStory: This is the exposure of hidden idolatry and the limit of even the greatest human righteousness, unable to save anyone beyond itself. Every page after this magnifies the wonder that Christ's righteousness breaks that very limit, becoming the one righteousness in history that genuinely does deliver others, not merely Himself, from judgment we justly deserve.

context.literary:
Chapter 14 is built as two oracles, each opened by the formula 'the word of the LORD came to me,' at verse 2 and verse 12, and joined by the single question that runs through them both: what use is a relationship with God that has been emptied of its center? The first oracle, verses 1 to 11, is a case law. A man sets up idols in his heart and then comes to inquire of the LORD. The same statement, almost word for word, is given three times, in verses 3, 4 and 7, each time moving outward, from the elders to 'any Israelite' to 'any foreigner dwelling in Israel.' The effect is of a rule being widened step by step until no one is left outside it.

The second oracle is an argument built on a fourfold list. In verses 13 to 20 a land sins, and God sends in turn famine, wild beasts, the sword and plague. Each time the response is the same: even if Noah, Daniel and Job stood there, 'they could not deliver their own sons or daughters.' The refrain is repeated in verses 14, 16, 18 and 20, with the oath 'as surely as I live' in the last three. The rhythm is meant to wear down every escape route, one possible disaster after another.

Then verse 21 collapses the four hypotheticals into a single event: 'How much worse will it be when I send against Jerusalem My four dire judgments.' The earlier verses spoke of 'a land'; this one names Jerusalem. The argument has been a conditional that closes on a fact. Verses 22 and 23 end the chapter with a surprising turn, a group of survivors whose coming out will bring comfort. The chapter therefore moves from inward sin to outward calamity to a remnant, and its two halves answer each other: the first asks who may consult God, the second asks who may stand between God and a guilty land.
context.historical:
Elders of Israel had visited Ezekiel before, in his own house in the sixth year, Ezekiel 8:1, and again in the seventh year, Ezekiel 20:1, which says they 'came to inquire of the LORD.' In exile there was no temple, no altar and no priest at hand, so the elders were the leaders of the community and the prophet became the available channel to God. Their visit here would have looked like pious inquiry. They wanted a word about what would happen to Jerusalem, which still stood. The chapter's point is that the form of the visit conceals what is in the heart.

The three men named in verse 14 were not contemporaries of one another but figures of righteousness from different ages. Noah belonged to the primeval story, Genesis 6:9, and had saved his family in the ark, Genesis 7:1. Job was an upright man from the land of Uz, Job 1:1, and the book bearing his name shows him interceding for his friends, Job 42:8. Daniel is the third, and the reading with the most support among interpreters is the Judean Daniel of Daniel 1:6, who by now was in Babylon, a young man of exceptional reputation. The effect is a list of three men who were each remembered as saved from a catastrophe or as a successful intercessor.

The four judgments are the covenant curses of Leviticus 26:21-26 and Deuteronomy 32:24-25, in which sword, famine, wild animals and plague fall on a disobedient people. Ezekiel had already announced them in Ezekiel 5:17, and in chapter 12 verse 16 God had promised to spare a few from sword, famine and plague. Those curses were not novel threats; they were the penalties Israel had agreed to at Sinai. In 586 BC the sword and the famine arrived with the Babylonian siege, and the survivors who walked into exile, as Ezekiel 14:22 foresees, became the living evidence of the justice of what had happened.
context.canonical:
The first oracle belongs to a body of teaching in Israel about sin and prayer. Psalm 66:18 says, 'If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened.' Proverbs 28:9 says that whoever turns his ear from the law, 'even his prayer is detestable.' Isaiah 1:15 has God hiding His eyes from outstretched hands that are 'covered with blood.' Jeremiah 14:11-12 has Him refusing to hear fasting and offerings from a people He has abandoned. Ezekiel 14 gives the clearest case where the offense is not murder but idolatry of the heart. Jesus takes it into the Gospels when He quotes Isaiah against those who 'honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me,' Matthew 15:8, and then says that evil things come 'out of the heart,' Matthew 15:19. Paul calls greed 'idolatry,' Colossians 3:5, and John ends his first letter, 'keep yourselves from idols,' 1 John 5:21.

The second oracle belongs to the story of intercession. Abraham pleaded for Sodom, Genesis 18, and Moses for Israel, Exodus 32:11. The Lord told Jeremiah not to pray for the people, Jeremiah 7:16, and said that even if Moses and Samuel stood before Him His heart would not go out to them, Jeremiah 15:1. Ezekiel 14 gives the doctrine behind those hard words: when a people persist in sin, no one's righteousness can be credited to another. Ezekiel 18:20 states the principle for individuals, and chapter 22 verse 30 records God's search for someone to stand in the gap, finding no one.

The New Testament answers both. Romans 5:19 sets the obedience of one man against the disobedience of another, and Hebrews 7:25 says Jesus lives to intercede. The limit Ezekiel marks is real for every merely human righteousness, which is why a righteousness that is 'from God' is needed, Philippians 3:9.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel set out to take away two false securities from a community that had lost its temple but kept its religion. The first is the security of access. The elders thought that sitting before a prophet was a way of keeping in touch with God. Ezekiel's word is that God will answer a man who comes with idols in his heart, but He will answer him as a judge, 'in keeping with his many idols,' and not as a friend. Verse 5 reveals the purpose: God answers so 'that I may take hold of the hearts of the people of Israel.' The aim is not to punish the visitor but to seize the heart that has gone elsewhere.

The second false security is the credit of the righteous. A community that knew about Noah and Job could easily suppose that a few good people in the city would shield the rest. Ezekiel's oath, 'as surely as I live,' closes that door, since the righteous would save only themselves. The point is not that the righteous are of no value; it is that the nation cannot lean on them in place of its own repentance, verse 6.

And the chapter is also a call. 'Repent and turn away from your idols,' verse 6, is the command before the oracle of judgment even runs its course. Verse 11 states the goal in covenant words, 'Then they will be My people and I will be their God.' Ezekiel wanted his hearers to see that the sentence is itself a means of restoration, and that the survivors of verses 22 and 23 will be the proof that the judgment was not arbitrary.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes how God dealt with Israel's elders and with the land under Babylonian judgment. It does not give a rule that God never hears the prayers of the troubled or that a believer's sin silences Him. The Bible elsewhere shows God hearing the cry of those who come with broken hearts, Psalm 51:17, and the repentant tax collector in Luke 18:13 goes home justified. What Ezekiel condemns is the divided heart that wants an oracle from God and a place for idols too.

The list of Noah, Daniel and Job describes God's refusal to be moved by intercession in that one situation. It is not a prohibition against interceding for others. Paul urges prayer for everyone, 1 Timothy 2:1, and James says the prayer of a righteous person is powerful, James 5:16. Ezekiel is describing a case in which the guilt has gone so far that even a Noah could save only himself, and nothing in the passage says that is the normal condition of a believing community.

The lessons that do carry over are two. First, we should examine what is set up in the heart before we come to ask something of God, as the elders did not, 1 John 5:21. Second, no human righteousness, our own or another person's, is the ground of salvation for a family, a church or a nation. Descriptive statements about families, such as that children could not be rescued by a parent's righteousness, are not a rule about the eternal fate of any particular child.

debates.question: How can God say that He enticed the prophet in verse 9?

views.label: God ordains deceit as judgment on the inquirer
views.case: The verb is the one used in 1 Kings 22:20-23, where the LORD sends a lying spirit to entice Ahab, and in Jeremiah 20:7. God is not the author of sin but sovereign over it, and He hands a person who has chosen idols the false word he wanted. Romans 1:24-28 and 2 Thessalonians 2:11 describe the same pattern of God giving people over. The prophet is still punished, verse 10, because his own choice was real.

views.label: A Hebrew idiom of permission
views.case: Hebrew often attributes to God what He allows to happen. Verse 9 then means the LORD permits the prophet to be enticed, in the same way Pharaoh's hardening is attributed to Him. On this reading the stress falls on human responsibility, since the prophet is destroyed 'from among My people' for speaking when he was not sent.

debates.bearing: The text holds the sovereignty of God and the responsibility of the speaker together. Neither reading lets the false prophet off, and neither makes God the source of evil. The warning for anyone who seeks a favorable word is that God can let him hear exactly what his heart has asked for.

debates.question: Who is the Daniel of verse 14?

views.label: The Daniel of the exile
views.case: He is a contemporary of Ezekiel who was taken to Babylon in 605 BC and already famous for wisdom and integrity, Daniel 1:6. Ezekiel also mentions him in 28:3 as a model of wisdom. The pairing of a contemporary with Noah and Job would be striking, but it fits Ezekiel's habit of reaching for the best known figures.

views.label: An ancient righteous figure from Canaanite tradition
views.case: Some scholars point to a legendary righteous king named Danel known from the Ugaritic texts, who judged the cause of the widow and the orphan. On this view the three men are all ancient worthies, which fits Noah and Job better than a living young man would.

debates.bearing: Nothing in the argument turns on the identity. The three stand for the highest examples of righteousness any hearer could name, and the point is that even their combined merit could not rescue a single child.

debates.question: Who are the survivors of verses 22 and 23?

views.label: Righteous survivors who vindicate God
views.case: Their conduct would comfort the exiles by showing that the righteous are spared and that God's dealings are just.

views.label: Guilty survivors whose conduct explains the judgment
views.case: Verse 22 says the exiles will see 'their conduct and actions' and 'know that it was not without cause' that God acted. Many readers take this to mean the survivors are as corrupt as those who died, and that seeing them will convince the exiles the judgment was deserved, as in Ezekiel 12:16.

debates.bearing: Either way the survivors serve as witnesses to the justice of God. The second reading also shows that survival is by mercy, not merit, which fits the chapter's whole argument that righteousness cannot be transferred or earned.

study.originalLanguages:
The most striking phrase is in verse 3, where the men have 'set up idols in their hearts.' The verb is literally 'caused to go up,' as if they had lifted the idols onto a shrine inside themselves, and the noun gillulim is Ezekiel's preferred word for idols. Alongside the idols stands the 'stumbling block,' mikshol, in the phrase 'the stumbling block of their iniquity,' which in Ezekiel is something a person trips over on the way to ruin, Ezekiel 7:19 and 18:30. The BSB renders it a 'wicked stumbling block before his face.' The idol is placed in front of the eyes where it blocks the way to God.

Verse 3 also contains a rhetorical question built on the same verb twice. 'Should I consult with them?' translates a construction in which an infinitive stands before the finite verb, 'Shall I be sought, sought by them?' The doubling is emphatic and carries the force of 'surely not.' The verb darash, to seek or inquire, is the ordinary word for consulting God through a prophet. God's answer, in verse 4, plays on it: He will answer, but the Hebrew adds that He answers 'in keeping with the multitude of his idols,' which the BSB leaves implied. The reply is shaped by the inquirer's divided heart.

In verse 5 the purpose clause says God acts 'so that I may take hold of the hearts.' The verb tafas means to seize or grasp, the word used of catching a person or capturing a city. The same sentence says the people are 'estranged' from Me, a word describing something that has become foreign. God's judgment is a rescue of the heart that has been alienated.

In verse 9 the verb 'enticed' is patah, to persuade or deceive by a seductive appeal. It is used of the lying spirit sent to Ahab, 1 Kings 22:20-22, and of Jeremiah's complaint 'You enticed me,' Jeremiah 20:7. The Hebrew thus raises the moral question directly, and the wording makes the prophet's fall a matter of divine judgment as well as human weakness.

Verses 13 and 14 say a land 'acts unfaithfully,' and the Hebrew places the verb ma'al beside its own noun, 'unfaithfully unfaithful,' an emphatic form for deliberate breach of trust. It is the same root that will drive chapters 15 and 17. Finally the oath formula 'as surely as I live' in verses 16, 18 and 20 is the strongest oath God swears, drawn from His own existence, and its repetition three times ends any hope of exception.

typology.type: Noah, Daniel and Job as the limit of human righteousness, Ezekiel 14:14-20
typology.fulfillment: Each of the three was a righteous man who passed through judgment, Noah in the flood, Job in suffering, Daniel in exile. Ezekiel says the best of them could deliver only themselves. In Christ the limit is broken. Paul says that 'through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous,' Romans 5:19, and Isaiah's Servant 'will justify many,' Isaiah 53:11. The type is faithful in showing the need for a righteousness that can be shared, and it falls short because none of the three could offer a righteousness for another, while Christ did, 2 Corinthians 5:21.

typology.type: Idols in the heart and the stumbling block before the face, Ezekiel 14:3-7
typology.fulfillment: The idea that idolatry lives in the heart before it appears in any shrine is taken up by Jesus, who says evil comes out of the heart, Matthew 15:19, and by Paul, who names greed as idolatry, Colossians 3:5. The remedy promised by Ezekiel himself is a heart transplant: 'I will give you a new heart,' Ezekiel 36:26, and cleansing from 'all your idols,' Ezekiel 36:25. The New Testament fulfills this in the Spirit's indwelling, John 3:5-8 and Romans 8:9. The type is partial because the old covenant exposed the idol without removing it.

typology.type: The remnant brought out of the city, Ezekiel 14:22
typology.fulfillment: The survivors who 'come out' of the doomed city are a small portent of the greater remnant. Paul says, 'at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace,' Romans 11:5, and Jesus warns of the destruction of Jerusalem and tells His followers to leave it, Luke 21:20-21. The pattern is that a few are spared by mercy and are sent out to bear witness. It falls short of the final gathering, since the remnant here is saved from a catastrophe, while the redeemed in Christ are saved from the judgment that is yet to come.

study.christ:
Ezekiel 14 sets up a problem that only Christ can answer. If the greatest righteous people can rescue only themselves, who can rescue the guilty? The passage never says that no one can, only that none of these three can. Its silence is the opening through which the New Testament comes. Isaiah 53:11 speaks of a righteous Servant who 'will justify many.' Paul's reasoning in Romans 5:19 reads almost as a direct reply: the obedience of one man makes the many righteous. The Servant does what Noah, Daniel and Job could not, because His righteousness is not a personal asset that stays with Him but a gift that He bears on behalf of others.

The same logic appears in 2 Corinthians 5:21, 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' and in 1 Peter 3:18, 'the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God.' Ezekiel's three men were righteous and could not be substituted for anyone; Jesus is righteous and is substituted for everyone who trusts Him. The limit of verse 20, 'their righteousness could deliver only themselves,' is the exact limit that the cross removes.

The chapter also leads to Christ by the picture of intercession. The three men could not turn God from a guilty land, and Jeremiah 15:1 says that even Moses and Samuel could not. In Hebrews, Jesus lives to intercede for those who draw near, Hebrews 7:25, and Romans 8:34 says that He is interceding for us at the right hand of God. Isaiah 59:16 says God saw there was no one to intercede, so His own arm brought salvation. In the person of the Son, God supplies the intercessor He had not found.

The first oracle also points to Him. The elders came to inquire of the LORD and were met by a God who sees through the visit. Jesus says that people honor God with their lips while their hearts are far, Matthew 15:8, and He is the one who gives the cure Ezekiel promised, a new heart and the Spirit, Ezekiel 36:26-27. Where the elders carried idols in their hearts, the believer carries the Spirit, and 'a single offering' has made perfect those who are being sanctified, Hebrews 10:14.

One caution: the three men are not themselves types of Christ, and one should not read the flood, the whirlwind or the lions' den as secret Gospel. The chapter leads to Christ by showing the need, and the New Testament names the solution.
study.god:
The chapter shows, first, a God who looks at the heart. The elders had the right posture, sitting before the prophet, and the wrong interior. God reads past the visit and says, 'these men have set up idols in their hearts,' verse 3. In Ezekiel 33:31 He observes of the same sort of audience that they come, sit and listen but their hearts pursue gain. He is not deceived by appearances and does not accept worship that is only external.

It shows a God who answers on His terms. His reply to the idolater is not silence but judgment that is meant to recover him, 'so that I may take hold of the hearts of the people of Israel,' verse 5. Even when He refuses to be consulted as a friend, He is still pursuing His people. The language of 'take hold' is the language of a jealous love that will not let go, and the call to 'Repent and turn away from your idols' in verse 6 is itself an act of mercy before judgment.

It shows a God who is just in a measured, covenant way. The four judgments are the ones He had promised at Sinai, so He is acting on what He said, not out of caprice. Each hypothetical begins with a land that acts unfaithfully, verse 13, so judgment is the answer to a real fault. And God swears on His own life, 'as surely as I live,' three times, to show that His determination is not shaken by the presence of righteous men.

It shows a God who is not bought by credit from others. This is where the chapter presses on the doctrine. Divine justice does not treat righteousness as a bank account that can be drawn on for the guilty. At the same time, the Lord is no enemy of the righteous: Noah, Daniel and Job are saved, verses 14 and 20. He is the God who rescues those who belong to Him even while the land burns.

It shows a God who is sovereign over the false word. Verse 9 says He enticed the prophet, and the claim is difficult. It tells us that even deceit falls under His rule and serves His purposes of judgment, without implying that He is the author of evil, as the verbs in verse 10 make plain: both prophet and inquirer 'bear their punishment.'

Finally, it shows a God who keeps the remnant for the sake of His name. Verses 22 and 23 spare some, so that the exiles will 'know that it was not without cause.' He is vindicated by what He does. For worship, this means coming to Him with what is actually in the heart, including what we are tempted to hide, and trusting Him to take hold of it.

crossReferences.note: God shows Ezekiel what the elders do in the dark, each at the shrine of his own idol, saying that the LORD does not see them. It is the hidden background to the elders who sit down before Ezekiel in 14:1, and explains why God says the idols are in their hearts.

The companion text on individual responsibility: the soul who sins is the one who dies, a son does not bear the father's iniquity, and the righteousness of the righteous falls upon him. Chapter 14's refusal to transfer righteousness to sons and daughters is the same principle.

Another case of people who come and sit before Ezekiel and hear his words but do not act on them. Their mouths express love while their hearts pursue gain, so it describes the exact condition of the elders of 14:1-3.

Even if Moses and Samuel stood before the LORD, His heart would not go out to this people. It is the parallel to Noah, Daniel and Job, showing that the greatest intercessors in Israel's memory would not turn judgment aside once the people had passed the point of return.

The covenant curses in their original form: plagues, wild animals that rob children, the sword and a cut supply of bread. Ezekiel's four dire judgments are these curses, so what he announces is the covenant at work, not a new threat.

The LORD tells Noah to enter the ark because He has found him righteous in this generation. Noah's righteousness saved his household in Genesis, so Ezekiel's claim that even he could save only himself is harder, and it shows how much worse the case of Jerusalem is.

God says Job's prayer will be accepted for his friends. Job is a real intercessor, and yet Ezekiel says that in a guilty land his righteousness would deliver only himself. Together the two texts show that intercession works within the limits God sets.

Through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, and through the obedience of one man many will be made righteous. It supplies the answer to the limit Ezekiel sets: here is a righteousness that does reach others.
God's righteous Servant will justify many and bear their iniquities. Where the three righteous men can deliver only themselves, the Servant bears the guilt of others and gives them His righteousness.

God's answer to idols in the heart: He will cleanse them from all their idols, give a new heart and put His Spirit within them. What 14:5 says about taking hold of the heart is carried through here by renewal.

study.oneStory:
Ezekiel 14 sits at a turn in the book where the reader has just seen the glory leave the temple and now learns why God no longer answers as before. The question it answers goes back to Eden. In Genesis 3 the man and the woman hide, and God comes asking where they are. In Ezekiel 14 the elders approach God and He asks whether He should be consulted at all. The relation between God and a people that carry rival loves in their hearts is broken in the same way, and what is lost in both cases is the free coming and going that God intended.

The chapter also answers a question that arises from earlier chapters: why did intercession not rescue the nation? Abraham pleaded for Sodom, Moses saved Israel after the golden calf, and Samuel prayed in crisis. Ezekiel's three men carry the same line of mediators, and he declares that this time they would not suffice. The covenant had been broken for too long, and the curses promised at Sinai in Leviticus 26 had to be seen to be real.

But the chapter sets up the story of redemption by naming the need. If the best men cannot rescue anyone, then someone else must. Ezekiel's own later chapters answer by promising a new heart, a new Spirit and an everlasting covenant of peace, Ezekiel 36:26-27 and 37:26, and the prophets after him promise the Servant who justifies many, Isaiah 53:11. Jeremiah promises the law written on hearts, Jeremiah 31:33, which is the cure for the idols that had set up house there.

The story comes to its center in Christ, whose obedience gives righteousness to others, Romans 5:19, and who intercedes without end, Hebrews 7:25. The apostles carry the warning forward, telling believers to keep themselves from idols, 1 John 5:21, because the heart remains a place where rivals can settle.

It ends in the new creation. In Revelation 21 and 22 there is no idolatry and no stumbling block. 'Nothing impure' will enter the city, and the people of God will see His face, Revelation 22:4. The remnant who walked out of Jerusalem are a small sign of the vast company who come out of the great tribulation and stand before the throne, Revelation 7:9-14. The elders who sat before the prophet with idols in their hearts are answered by a people whose hearts have been cleansed and who sit before God Himself.

sermon.title: Genuine or False Prophets? (Ezek. 13-14)
sermon.why: Carson's exposition spans both chapters 13 and 14, addressing how idols set up in the heart, chapter 14, corrupt even sincere-looking inquiry of God, the same theme of hidden versus genuine spiritual reality that runs through his treatment of false prophecy in chapter 13.

quiz.q: What is the specific hypocrisy God exposes in the elders who come to Ezekiel?

options.text: They have set up idols in their hearts while outwardly coming to inquire of the LORD through His prophet.
options.note: Verse 3 states this exact charge, exposing an inward idolatry hidden behind an outward, pious act.

options.text: They refused to visit Ezekiel at all.
options.note: The elders do come and sit before Ezekiel; the problem is what they carry in their hearts while doing so.

options.text: They openly worshiped idols in the temple courts.
options.note: The idolatry described here is specifically inward, 'in their hearts', not a described public temple scene.

options.text: They demanded that Ezekiel perform miracles to prove his prophetic authority.
options.note: Their sin is hidden idolatry while inquiring of God, not a demand for miraculous proof.

quiz.q: According to verses 12-20, what could the righteousness of Noah, Daniel, and Job accomplish for a sinning land under judgment?

options.text: It could deliver only themselves, not even their own sons or daughters.
options.note: This exact phrase is repeated multiple times across verses 14, 16, 18, and 20.

options.text: It could deliver the entire land from judgment.
options.note: The passage explicitly denies this; their righteousness saves only themselves.

options.text: It could delay judgment for one generation.
options.note: The text speaks of personal deliverance, not a delay of judgment for the land.

options.text: It could deliver their immediate family but not the wider community.
options.note: The text is stronger still: even their own sons and daughters could not be delivered by their righteousness.

quiz.q: What are the four dire judgments named in verse 21?

options.text: Sword, famine, wild beasts, and plague.
options.note: Verse 21 lists exactly these four judgments against Jerusalem.

options.text: Fire, flood, earthquake, and drought.
options.note: These are not the four judgments named in this passage.

options.text: Exile, imprisonment, poverty, and disease.
options.note: These general categories do not match the specific four judgments the text names.

options.text: Sword, famine, exile, and shame.
options.note: Two of these overlap with the actual list, but 'wild beasts' and 'plague' are the accurate remaining judgments, not 'exile' and 'shame'.

quiz.q: What comfort does God promise regarding the survivors who come out of Jerusalem's judgment?

options.text: Their conduct and actions will bring comfort by showing the judgment was not without cause.
options.note: Verses 22-23 state that seeing their conduct will bring consolation and confirm the justice of God's actions.

options.text: They will be exempt from ever explaining what happened.
options.note: The text says the opposite; their visible conduct becomes a testimony to why judgment fell.

options.text: They will immediately rebuild Jerusalem's temple.
options.note: The passage focuses on their conduct providing comfort and confirmation, not a rebuilding project.

options.text: They will be given new names to hide their past.
options.note: No mention of new names is made; the comfort comes from witnessing their sobered conduct.

quiz.q: What theological principle does this chapter establish about righteousness and judgment?

options.text: Human righteousness, however great, cannot be transferred to deliver others from judgment justly deserved by a land.
options.note: The extended argument using Noah, Daniel, and Job establishes exactly this principle.

options.text: Any righteous person automatically protects their entire community from judgment.
options.note: The passage explicitly denies this; righteousness here delivers only the individual.

options.text: God never judges a land as long as one righteous person remains in it.
options.note: The text describes judgment falling even with righteous individuals present; they alone are personally spared.

options.text: Righteousness matters only for religious leaders, not ordinary people.
options.note: The principle applies to individual standing before God generally, not merely to leaders.

questions: The elders sought God's word while secretly harboring idols in their hearts. What might you be carrying in your own heart that quietly competes with genuine devotion to God, even while you look for His guidance?

Even Noah, Daniel, and Job could not save others by their own righteousness. Where might you be relying on someone else's faith or character, a parent, spouse, or mentor, rather than your own relationship with Christ?

God promises that the remnant's visible, sobered conduct will bring comfort even amid deserved judgment. How might your own changed life, after failure or discipline, become a source of comfort and testimony to others?

This chapter shows the real limits of human righteousness contrasted with the limitless righteousness of Christ. How does resting in Christ's righteousness, rather than your own performance, change the way you approach your own failures?
God says He will 'take hold of the hearts' of His people through this confrontation. Where do you need God to take hold of your heart and expose an idol you have not yet named honestly?

translationNotes.note: Scholars debate whether 'Daniel' here refers to the biblical prophet, Ezekiel's approximate contemporary, or an ancient legendary figure named Danel known from other ancient Near Eastern texts; either way the three names together form a proverbial trio of righteousness.
